title: Live Streaming (Twitch)
summary: Design a live video platform with broadcaster ingest, real-time delivery to large audiences, and live chat.
statement: Design a live streaming service. Broadcasters stream from their devices; viewers watch with low latency and chat in real time. A single stream may have hundreds of thousands of viewers. Start by clarifying requirements and estimating scale, then design the system and defend your decisions.
initialGuidance: Clarify the users, the main journeys, and what is explicitly out of scope before drawing anything.
Estimate read and write volume and storage growth; the numbers decide which components you need.
Name the guarantees you will offer (consistency, durability, availability) and the trade-offs behind them.
Write down assumptions as you make them and revisit them when requirements change.
coreFunctionalRequirements: Deliver streams to viewers with low delay.
List live channels and viewer counts.

requirementQuestions.question: What glass-to-glass delay is acceptable: several seconds or sub-second?
requirementQuestions.whyItMatters: Defines which paths need caching, precomputation, or regional placement.

requirementQuestions.question: How many concurrent streams and the largest audience for one stream?
requirementQuestions.whyItMatters: Sets read and write rates and storage growth, which decide whether a single node can cope.

requirementQuestions.question: What happens if the broadcaster drops or an ingest node fails?
requirementQuestions.whyItMatters: Determines redundancy and failover design, and which features may degrade instead of failing.

requirementQuestions.question: Are recordings, clips, and interactive features required?
requirementQuestions.whyItMatters: Fixes what is in and out of the design so effort goes to what matters.

requirementQuestions.question: How is egress cost controlled for large audiences?
requirementQuestions.whyItMatters: Prevents over-engineering and affects build-versus-buy choices.

requirementQuestions.question: How are chat spam and prohibited streams handled in real time?
requirementQuestions.whyItMatters: Adds validation, rate limiting, and fraud controls to the critical path.

workloadAssumptions.illustrativeNote: All numbers below are illustrative examples for practice and are not benchmarks. Real answers depend on the requirements the candidate negotiates.

estimationPrompts: How much transcoding capacity do 100,000 streams need?
What egress does a 500,000-viewer stream generate?
How many chat messages per second must one large channel handle?

keyDecisions.question: How do streams enter the platform?
considerations: RTMP or modern ingest protocols to nearby ingest points.

keyDecisions.question: How are renditions produced in real time?
considerations: Compute cost scales with streams, not viewers.
Transcode only popular streams at full ladder.

keyDecisions.question: How is video sent to viewers?
considerations: WebRTC for ultra-low latency but more costly.
CDN fan-out to a huge audience.

keyDecisions.question: How does chat scale?
considerations: Pub/sub per channel with sharded connections.
Rate limits and message sampling in big rooms.

keyDecisions.question: How are recordings and listings produced?
considerations: Write segments to storage as the stream proceeds.
Viewer counts are approximate and aggregated.

tradeoffs.tension: Lower delay reduces CDN efficiency and increases cost.

tradeoffs.topic: Full ladder for all streams vs popular ones

tradeoffs.tension: Show every message versus sampling in huge rooms.

commonMistakes: Pushing video through a single server per stream to all viewers.
Treating live like VOD with long segments and high delay.
One global chat server for all channels.
followUps: How do you reduce latency to under two seconds?
How do you create clips from a live stream?
How do you handle a raid that moves 100,000 viewers instantly?
How do you do regional failover for ingest?
